Turkey giveaways continue, even as rising prices squeeze nonprofits

The cost of a turkey is up 14% compared to 2025, cutting into budget lines for charitable traditions.
by Maddie Robinson 23 hours ago11/25/2026

Outside of Union Gospel Mission Twin Cities (UGMTC) in St. Paul on Monday, a line of cars stretched down the block, each with passengers waiting their turn to receive a free bag of Thanksgiving groceries. 

Volunteers, bundled up in coats, hats and gloves, handed drivers a turkey, a five-pound bag of potatoes, rice, stuffing and a dessert mix. In all, UGMTC doled out 2,000 grocery bags as part of the annual event, each with enough food to feed five people.

As cars weaved through makeshift lanes, community relations director Sarah Peterka bustled around the busy parking lot. “I just checked our semi. The semi is empty, and the last pallet of turkeys is sitting out, and so it’s going to be tight,” she said. “I don’t know if we’re gonna have a lot of leftovers.” 

UGMTC’s Thanksgiving event is one of many food and meal distribution programs in the Twin Cities this year, alongside the Salvation Army, the Thielen Foundation, the Sanneh Foundation and more. Some deliver groceries, others host Thanksgiving meals. And this year, nearly all of them are facing higher costs and higher demand. 

Registrations for UGMTC’s Thanksgiving food distribution have been filling up more quickly each year, Peterka said. This year, slots filled up the same weekend they opened in October. 

The cost of rising costs

In Minnesota, the cost of a 10-person “traditional” Thanksgiving dinner – including turkey, stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls, cranberries and pumpkin pie – costs about $63.33, up 4% from 2025, according to the Minnesota Farm Bureau’s annual survey.

Organizations like UGMTC feel the effects. While congregations and community partners provide the side dishes, UGMTC typically budgets $75,000-$85,000 to purchase the turkeys, Peterka said. This year, turkeys are driving the rising costs – a 16-pound frozen turkey costs $27.08, up 14% from 2025. 

One of Peterka’s first years at UGMTC coincided with a particularly bad bird flu outbreak, resulting in a $125,000 turkey bill.

“So you’re standing with your CFO, and you’re going, ‘Okay, this is like $125,000,’” she said. “It’s one of those things where you say, ‘This is a good thing. This is something where we show the community we’re here to help in more ways than just basic needs and a safe place for someone to sleep.’”

Still, there were Thanksgivings more than a decade ago when UGMTC could afford to give out anywhere from 5,000 to 10,000 turkeys, she said.

9 million food shelf visits

Thanksgiving arrives in 2026 as food shelves across Minnesota are on track for a fifth consecutive year of record-breaking demand, said Sophia Lenarz-Coy, executive director of The Food Group, a nonprofit focused on food accessibility. 

Minnesotans made nine million visits to food shelves last year, a 151% increase from 2019, Lenarz-Coy said. She attributed the increase to rising gas and grocery prices and cuts to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).

As cars wound through the UGMTC parking lot, a group of volunteers from the nearby Christ Recovery Center residential treatment facility handed out turkeys and wished drivers a happy holiday. Volunteer Mike Patsy said giving back to people who need the assistance is his favorite part of the event.

“It changes some of these people’s lives that come through here,” he said.

A note about the data: The figures used in the graph above come from Feeding America, a national nonprofit aimed at alleviating hunger. Feeding America estimates county-level food insecurity rates using national survey data and local measures such as poverty, unemployment, homeownership and disability rates. These figures are estimates, not direct counts, providing a snapshot of food insecurity in the region. 

Shay Scanlan contributed reporting to this story. She is a journalism student at the University of Minnesota, an editor at the Minnesota Daily and a reporting intern at MinnPost.
